title: Liverwort
wiki_lead:
Liverworts are non-vascular land plants in the division Marchantiophyta ( ). Liverworts, mosses, and hornworts are collectively known as bryophytes. Like mosses and hornworts, liverworts have a gametophyte-dominant life cycle in which the sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte.
Some liverworts have a flat branching thallus, while others are leafy. They are distinguished from mosses by their single-celled rhizoids, the absence of a midrib or costa in the leaves, and the presence of membrane-bound complex oil bodies.
There are an estimated 9,000 species of liverworts, most of them leafy. They occur in many terrestrial ecosystems worldwide, especially in moist tropical regions, although some are adapted to deserts and other dry environments.

Liverworts are non-vascular land plants in the division Marchantiophyta ( ). Liverworts, mosses, and hornworts are collectively known as bryophytes. Like mosses and hornworts, liverworts have a gametophyte-dominant life cycle in which the sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte.
Some liverworts have a flat branching thallus, while others are leafy. They are distinguished from mosses by their single-celled rhizoids, the absence of a midrib or costa in the leaves, and the presence of membrane-bound complex oil bodies.
There are an estimated 9,000 species of liverworts, most of them leafy. They occur in many terrestrial ecosystems worldwide, especially in moist tropical regions, although some are adapted to deserts and other dry environments.


Physical characteristics


Description
Most liverworts are small, from 2 to 20 millimetres (0.08 to 0.8 in) wide with individual plants less than 10 centimetres (4 in) long, so they are often overlooked. The most familiar liverworts, in the order Marchantiales, consist of a prostrate, flattened, ribbon-like or branching structure called a thallus (plant body). However, most liverworts produce flattened stems with overlapping scales or leaves in two or more ranks, the middle rank is often conspicuously different from the outer ranks; these leafy liverworts are in the order Jungermanniales.


Recognition
Liverworts can most reliably be distinguished from similar-looking mosses by their single-celled rhizoids. Other differences are not universal for all mosses and liverworts, but the lack of clearly differentiated stem and leaves in species with a thallus, or deeply lobed or segmented leaves and the presence of leaves arranged in three ranks in leafy species, the absence of a midrib or costa in the leaves, and frequent dichotomous branching all point to the plant's being a liverwort. With a few exceptions, all liverworts undergo polyplastidic meiosis, in contrast to mosses and hornworts which have monoplastidic meiosis. Unlike any other embryophytes, most liverworts contain complex oil bodies containing isoprenoids and surrounded by membranes in some of their cells.


Life cycle


Sexual

Liverworts, like other bryophytes, have a gametophyte-dominant life cycle, with the sporophyte dependent on the gametophyte. The sporophytes of many but not all liverworts are non-photosynthetic. Cells of the gametophyte plant each contain only a single set of genetic information, so liverworts are haploid for the majority of their life cycle. This contrasts sharply with the pattern in seed plants, where the haploid generation is represented only by the tiny pollen and ovule, while the diploid generation is the familiar plant. Another unusual feature is that the sporophytes (i.e. the diploid body) are very short-lived, withering away soon after releasing their spores.

The life of a liverwort starts when a haploid spore germinates to produce a transitory protonema, which is either a mass of thread-like filaments or a flattened thallus. The protonema grows into a mature gametophyte plant that produces the sex organs. The male organ is known as an antheridium; it produces sperm cells. The female organ is known as an archegonium. Each archegonium has a slender hollow tube or neck down which the sperm swim to reach the egg cell.
Liverwort species may be either dioicous or monoicous. In dioicous liverworts, female and male sex organs are borne on different and separate gametophyte plants. In monoicous liverworts, the two kinds of reproductive structures are borne on different branches of the same plant. In either case, the sperm must move from the antheridia where they are produced to the archegonium where the eggs are held. The sperm of liverworts have two tail-like flagella that enable them to swim short distances.
